title: What Are UCITS? Meaning, Rules and Funds for Indians | Paasa
summary: What are UCITS? Learn what UCITS means, how UCITS ETFs work and why Indian investors buy them. UCITS are the EU rules that govern funds and ETFs.
body_markdown:
UCITS stands for Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities, the EU rulebook for investment funds. Any ETF or mutual fund that follows these rules is a UCITS fund, whatever it holds, including US stocks.


Most large UCITS ETFs, such as CSPX, are[domiciled in Ireland](https://paasa.com/blog/why-most-ucits-etfs-are-domiciled-in-ireland) or Luxembourg.


Indian investors can invest in UCITS funds through a global brokerage account, under the RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS).

## Who regulates UCITS funds?


A UCITS fund is regulated by the financial regulator of the EU or EEA country where it is domiciled.


The Central Bank of Ireland regulates Irish UCITS funds, and the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF) regulates Luxembourg ones.


For how Irish and Luxembourg UCITS funds differ for Indian investors, see[Ireland vs Luxembourg UCITS](https://paasa.com/blog/ireland-vs-luxembourg-ucits-does-the-domicile-matter) .


Every UCITS regulator applies the same law, Directive 2009/65/EC, known as the UCITS Directive. This post follows the consolidated text of April 2026.


A UCITS fund authorised in one EU or EEA country can be sold across the EEA under the same rules. Fund managers call this the UCITS passport.


Note: the UCITS rules date back to Directive 85/611/EEC of 1985. Directive 2009/65/EC replaced it.


## What rules does a UCITS fund have to follow?


A UCITS fund has to follow five core rules, all set out in the UCITS Directive (Directive 2009/65/EC).


The best known is the 5/10/40 rule. A fund can put at most 5% of assets in one issuer (up to 10% where its home country allows), and holdings above 5% cannot together exceed 40% of the fund.


**UCITS rule** **What the UCITS Directive says** **Where it is set** **What it means for you**


5/10/40 rule A UCITS fund can invest no more than 5% of its assets in securities of one issuer. EU countries can raise this to 10%, but holdings above 5% together cannot exceed 40% of assets Article 52 of the UCITS Directive No single company can dominate the fund


Index fund exception A UCITS fund tracking a recognised index can hold up to 20% in one issuer, and up to 35% in one issuer in exceptional market conditions Article 53 of the UCITS Directive An S&P 500 UCITS ETF can hold Nvidia or Apple at index weight


Redemption on request A UCITS fund must buy back units at the request of any unit holder. For a UCITS ETF, keeping the exchange price close to NAV counts as equivalent Article 1(2) and Article 84 of the UCITS Directive You exit a UCITS mutual fund by redeeming with the fund, and a UCITS ETF by selling it on the exchange. A fund can suspend redemptions temporarily


Leverage limit A UCITS fund cannot borrow, except temporarily up to 10% of its assets where its home country allows it. Its global exposure to derivatives cannot exceed the total net value of its portfolio Article 51 and Article 83 of the UCITS Directive Limits how far the fund can magnify gains and losses


Independent depositary A UCITS fund appoints a single depositary to hold its assets, and the depositary can reuse them only under strict conditions Article 22 of the UCITS Directive Fund assets sit apart from the fund manager


For how these UCITS rules apply to S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 trackers, see[What are UCITS ETFs?](https://paasa.com/blog/what-are-ucits-etfs)


## Is a UCITS fund an ETF or a mutual fund?


Both. A UCITS fund can be an exchange-traded fund (ETF) or a mutual fund, and both follow the same UCITS Directive.


The difference between a UCITS ETF and a UCITS mutual fund is how you buy and sell it.


**UCITS ETF** **UCITS mutual fund**


Where you buy it On a stock exchange, such as the London Stock Exchange or Xetra From the fund manager or a distributor


Price you get Live market price during trading hours Net asset value (NAV), set after the dealing cut-off


When you can trade Any time the exchange is open On the fund's dealing days


Rulebook UCITS Directive (2009/65/EC) UCITS Directive (2009/65/EC)


For fees, minimums and when a UCITS mutual fund makes more sense than a UCITS ETF, see[UCITS mutual funds vs UCITS ETFs](https://paasa.com/blog/ucits-mutual-funds-vs-ucits-etf) .


## How can you check if a fund is UCITS?


Four checks confirm whether a fund is UCITS. All four use the fund provider's own documents or the regulator's register.


1. **The fund name.** UCITS ETFs usually carry "UCITS" in the name, such as iShares Core S&P 500 UCITS ETF. Many UCITS mutual funds don't, so rely on the next three checks for them.
2. **The key facts.** The fund provider's product page states UCITS status, domicile and the issuing company.
3. **The KID.** A UCITS fund sold to EU retail investors publishes a Key Information Document.
4. **The regulator.** The fund's home regulator authorises it, and the prospectus names that regulator, such as the Central Bank of Ireland for Irish funds.


Note: an ISIN starting with IE or LU shows that a fund is domiciled in Ireland or Luxembourg. It does not prove the fund is UCITS, because Ireland and Luxembourg also host non-UCITS funds.


**Example.** Suppose you are about to buy[CSPX](https://paasa.com/etfs/cspx-l) and want to confirm it is a UCITS fund. Here is what the iShares product page for CSPX shows, as of 21 October 2026.


**What CSPX shows**


Fund name iShares Core S&P 500 UCITS ETF USD (Acc)


UCITS status UCITS: Yes


ISIN IE00B5BMR087


Domicile Ireland


Issuer and regulator iShares VII plc, authorised by the Central Bank of Ireland


Listings CSPX (USD) and CSP1 (GBP) on the London Stock Exchange, SXR8 (EUR) on Xetra


**The result: CSPX passes all four checks.** CSPX is an Irish UCITS ETF, and the same fund trades in USD, GBP and EUR under different tickers. The ISIN, IE00B5BMR087, stays the same on every listing.

## Are UCITS funds safe?


Yes, UCITS funds are safe, but that does not mean they are risk-free. The UCITS Directive protects investors from how a fund is run, not from market losses.


**UCITS protects you from** **UCITS does not protect you from**


One company dominating the fund (5/10/40 rule, Article 52) A fall in the market the fund tracks


The fund manager using fund assets (independent depositary, Article 22) Currency moves between the fund's currency and the rupee


Heavy borrowing or derivatives leverage Tracking difference between the fund and its index


Being locked in: you can redeem a UCITS mutual fund on request or sell a UCITS ETF on the exchange (except during a temporary suspension) Wide bid-ask spreads on a thinly traded listing


## Indian investors and UCITS funds


Many Indian residents use Irish UCITS funds such as CSPX for US market exposure without US estate tax risk, because shares of an Irish fund are not US-situated assets.


Accumulating share classes add a second benefit: the fund reinvests dividends, so there is no yearly dividend income to tax in India.


[UCITS vs US ETFs for Indian investors](https://paasa.com/blog/ucits-for-indian-investors) compares the two in full, with a worked example, and[how US estate tax applies to Indians and NRIs](https://paasa.com/blog/how-us-estate-tax-works-for-indians-and-nris) covers the estate tax side.


Indian residents can buy UCITS funds under the RBI's[Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS)](https://paasa.com/blog/what-is-lrs-complete-guide) , which allows a resident individual to remit up to[USD 250,000 per financial year](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_CircularIndexDisplay.aspx?Id=9756) for permitted investments.


The[guide to UCITS ETFs](https://paasa.com/blog/what-are-ucits-etfs) explains how these funds work in practice, and[how to buy UCITS ETFs from India](https://paasa.com/blog/how-to-buy-ucits-etfs-from-india) walks through the process step by step.
